title: Geo‑entitlement routing & SLA mapping for enterprise residency requests
creator: Lena Zhou
description:
Problem: Enterprise customers request new region availability, data residency guarantees, and predictable failover behavior. We need a reproducible intake + routing + SLA mapping flow that lets Sales/Support quickly triage and produce a go/no-go recommendation and required engineering scope.

Goal: Define a tiered intake form, categorical routing rules, and an SLA/commitment matrix that translates customer ask -> product response -> engineering work estimate. Deliverables: intake form template, triage rubric, routing rules (eng, sales, legal, infra), example responses for customers, and a minimal dashboard for tracking open requests.

Scope and non‑scope: Includes: new region activation requests, residency-only requests, dedicated failover/DR requirements, and high‑value enterprise entitlements. Excludes: individual customer feature bugs and minor US/EU capacity adjustments that are handled by capacity ops.

Decision boundaries and routing logic (high level):
- Tier 0 (self-serve): requests that are satisfied by existing regions and standard failover config -> auto-reply with onboarding guide.
- Tier 1 (accelerated enablement): residency requests covered by our standard Private offering or Dedicated with minimal infra work -> route to Solutions Eng + Sales.
- Tier 2 (engineering work + compliance): requires infra changes (new region provisioning, network peering) or legal/regulatory review -> route to Product, Infra Eng, Security & Legal.
- Tier 3 (strategic / commercial exceptions): large contract or bespoke on‑prem deployments -> route to GTM lead + Enterprise Sales + Exec review.

SLA mapping matrix (example):
- Self‑serve: guidance + documented steps, no SLA.
- Accelerated enablement: 30 business day target to provision and validate, with standard onboarding checklist.
- Engineering+compliance: Target 90 business days (estimate), initial technical feasibility review within 7 business days.
- Strategic: timeline negotiated in commercial terms.

Required intake fields (minimum viable form): company name, region(s) requested, residency vs backup failover intent, data classification, compliance drivers (e.g., GDPR/CCPA/PDPA), expected throughput/latency SLOs, contract value / ARR, desired go‑live date, artifacts (SOC/ISO needs), point of contact.

Metrics to track: time to initial triage, time to technical decision, provisioning lead time, percentage routed to each tier, conversion rate (request -> active region), revenue attached.

Artifacts and links:
- Intake form draft (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PM/pages/Geo+Intake+Draft
- Example provisioning checklist (Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/example-provisioning-checklist
- Initial infra scoping RFC (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/198

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How prescriptive should SLA timelines be vs conservative estimates to avoid overpromising? (PM preference: conservative public timelines + internal prioritization lanes).
- Do we expose a public eligibility table to customers or keep routing logic internal? (Tradeoff: transparency vs increased support churn).
- Should small compliance-only requests be handled as separate fast path or folded into Tier 1? (Engineering time impact vs customer speed).

Next steps: finalize intake form (this ticket), align SLA matrix with Legal and Infra (follow-up workshop), prototype triage dashboard (Data & Analytics), and roll out to Sales/Support with training.
